title: Same Policy, Different Trajectories
subtitle: Consistency in long-horizon RL · Selectors and budgets · Reading NTK
intro: This issue examines training–sampling consistency in long-horizon RL and the budget boundaries of selection and feedback in 3D generation. Five papers/blogs and one technical follow-up are overlap-window additions, alongside two version records with unverified changes; none is presented as first released today. Our classic is NTK: from Jacobians to spectral filtering.

articles.title: Same weights, different policy
articles.dateNote: 2026-10-15 · overlap-window addition; QwenGyre and renderers below are background

blocks.text: Long-horizon RL mismatch extends beyond stale weights: tool parsing can change tokens, trajectory reconstruction can change contexts, and numerical kernels can change probabilities. The blog connects these failure modes across execution.[1]

blocks.label: Explanatory notation: cᵤ is the original context; equality also requires matching inputs, sampling distributions, and computation

blocks.text: QwenGyre retains recorded behavior probabilities instead of recomputing the denominator on the trainer, and deduplicates trainable tokens across an execution tree. It normalizes by execution rather than rewarding tasks with more branches:[2]

blocks.label: Original Appendix B; Lᵢ counts deduplicated target tokens, and ℓᵤ includes the advantage, clipping, and shared mask

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: Token-in/token-out prevents retokenization drift, not numerical mismatch by itself. Recomputing old log-probabilities to force a unit ratio does not change the actual sampling distribution into the trainer distribution.[1,3]

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: In a separate eight-input study, human-guided refinement achieves Full=8/8 but only 6/8 under strict criteria; parallel Oracle@8 reaches 3/8. Matching output counts does not match compute or human effort, so this does not establish compute-optimal recursive scaling.[4]

blocks.text: Using 1,000 hours of HumanTouch, retaining tactile pretraining supervision raises vision-only Ego Humanoid success from 52.5 to 71.7% against a same-data/compute baseline that discards touch. This tests supervision quality, not a fitted data-scaling exponent. Real-robot results also use deployment-time touch and have a different attribution.[6]

classic.paper: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
classic.authors: Arthur Jacot · Franck Gabriel · Clément Hongler
classic.title: NTK: nonlinear training becomes a linear flow
classic.dateNote: Historical classic: first posted 2018-06-20; read v4 dated 2020-02-10; NeurIPS 2018
classic.evidence: Read Sections 2–5, 6.1–6.2, and the appendix limit setup; checked the PDF theorem page
classic.question: Discussion: if \(\|K_t-K_0\|_{\rm op}/\|K_0\|_{\rm op}\) is small but \(\lambda_{\min}(K_0)\) is smaller still, are kernel predictions accurate on slow modes? Which relative drift should we measure?

blocks.text: NNGP (Lee et al., ICLR 2018) describes the function distribution at initialization.[13] NTK asks how functions move once optimization starts, separating nonlinear parameterization from dynamics on a finite training set.[11,12]

blocks.tex: f_t=(f_{\theta_t}(x_i))_{i=1}^n,\quad r_t=f_t-y,\quad J_t=\frac{\partial f_t}{\partial\theta},\quad \mathcal L=\frac{\|r_t\|^2}{2n},\qquad \dot r_t=-\frac1nK_t r_t,\quad K_t=J_tJ_t^\top
blocks.label: Scalar output and full-batch gradient flow; an exact finite-width chain-rule identity

blocks.text: Theorem 2 assumes fixed depth, Gaussian initialization, NTK parameterization, a Lipschitz twice-differentiable activation with bounded second derivative, sequential width limits, and a stochastically bounded time-integrated training direction. The kernel then becomes constant on finite time intervals.[11]

blocks.label: Original parameterization and a matrix formulation of the theorem on a fixed finite training set; T is fixed

blocks.text: With the kernel fixed, squared-loss dynamics form a linear constant-coefficient system. The next two formulas solve it directly, using orthonormal eigenvectors:[11]

blocks.tex: K_\infty v_j=\lambda_jv_j,\qquad r_t=e^{-tK_\infty/n}r_0=\sum_{j=1}^n e^{-\lambda_jt/n}\langle v_j,r_0\rangle v_j
blocks.label: Residuals with λ=0 persist; positive semidefiniteness alone does not ensure fitting every label
Direct consequence: early stopping is spectral filtering; large kernel eigenvalues learn first, not universally low input frequencies

blocks.text: Let \(k(x,X)\) be the limiting kernel row from a test point to the training set. When invertible, off-training predictions retain an initialization term:[11]

blocks.label: Obtained by integrating the training-set solution; scalar-output rewrite

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: Training convergence is not a generalization guarantee. Finite-width ReLU experiments do not remove Theorem 2’s smoothness assumptions; the fixed-kernel limit does not explain all finite-width feature learning.[11]

blocks.title: Discussion question
blocks.text: Discussion: if \(\|K_t-K_0\|_{\rm op}/\|K_0\|_{\rm op}\) is small but \(\lambda_{\min}(K_0)\) is smaller still, are kernel predictions accurate on slow modes? Which relative drift should we measure?
